n:
- In the year after Israel left Egypt, the Lord often communicated his will to the people through Moses, giving them many chances to follow his divine plan. 

- God often revealed himself *in the Tent of Meeting*; see study note on Exodus 27:21. 

- The wilderness of Sinai was a vast, frightening, and harsh desert ({{Deuteronomy 1:19|Deuteronomy 1:19}}). This mostly empty area was where God matured Israel. The challenges of Sinai's harsh living conditions tested Israel's reliance on the Lord throughout the book of Numbers. Sinai reminded later biblical authors of the law and Israel's rebellious spirit ({{Psalm 106:19|Psalm 106:19}}; {{Hebrews 12:25-26|Hebrews 12:25–26}}).
God chose a family leader from each tribe (except the tribe of Levi), to count Israel's men who were old enough to be soldiers.

The people of Israel camped at Mount Sinai for two years. God’s instructions to them while they were there are recorded in Exodus and Leviticus.

God’s instructions that are recorded in Numbers were about preparing to leave Mount Sinai. Moses, Aaron and the leaders of the 12 tribes of Israel counted the people.

First they counted the men 20 years old or older. These were men who could fight in battles. Moses counted the Levite males who were 30 to 50 years old. Moses also counted the males one month old or older in Levi’s tribe.

Then he counted the eldest sons in the other tribes. All Israelite males who were born first in their family belonged to God. The reason for this was explained in Exodus 11:1 – 13:16. This didn’t mean that God wanted the Israelites to sacrifice children. Instead, the Levite males took the place of the eldest sons from other tribes. They did this by being set apart to serve God.

Levite males from Aaron’s family line were set apart to serve God as priests. Others were responsible for taking care of the different parts of the holy tent.

The holy tent was in the centre of the Israelite camp. The tribes were arranged in order around it. First were the Levites who camped closest to the holy tent. Then came the tribe of Judah. They were the lead tribe and had the most soldiers. After that were the other Israelite tribes.

People who were considered unclean couldn’t be near the tent. They couldn’t even stay in the camp. This reminded the Israelites that God is holy and was present with them.
The Israelites got ready to leave for the promised land by listing all troops who could join the conquest. The nation was changing from slavery to becoming a nation.

- *those who are twenty years of age or older by their divisions—everyone who can serve in Israel’s army:* This registration gathered more information than the earlier census (compare {{Exodus 38:26|Exodus 38:26}}). 

- *These are the names of the men who are to assist you: *Hebrew culture was tribal, centered around clans and families. They easily identified the tribal leaders, who appear again as a group in {{Numbers 7:1-89|Numbers 7}}. 

- Moses and Aaron did not include the tribe of Levi in this registration because it had a special status in Israelite society (see {{Numbers 1:47-53|Numbers 1:47–53}}; {{Numbers 26:51-62|26:51–62}}; {{Deuteronomy 18:5|Deuteronomy 18:5}}; {{Deuteronomy 33:8-11|33:8–11}}).
These tribal leaders proved to be responsible and trustworthy by completing other important tasks.

The count of 603,550 shows the same number of qualified men as mentioned in {{Exodus 38:26|Exodus 38:26}}. {{Exodus 12:37|Exodus 12:37}} and {{Numbers 11:21|Numbers 11:21}} give an approximate number of 600,000. 

People have interpreted these numbers in different ways:

- The numbers might show the actual size of this army (see {{Exodus 1:9-10|Exodus 1:9–10}}). 

- The numbers might be symbolic. A later editor might have estimated, or might have misunderstood while translating. 

See also study note on Exodus 12:37.
The second list of tribes lists Gad with Reuben and Simeon. These two tribes camped with Gad while Israel traveled.
The tribe of Levi did not serve in Israel's army like the other tribes. This part of Numbers explains how the Levites organized to serve in the tabernacle of the Testimony, which was their main duty.
*tabernacle of the Testimony:* This was a portable sanctuary. It symbolized the Lord’s presence and showed Israel’s covenant relationship with him.

The Levites had the job of setting up, taking down, moving, and guarding the tabernacle. They kept unauthorized people from coming too close or making it unclean. This protected the Israelites from the Lord's judgment.

Israel organized its camps by tribal groups. This probably addressed social status, water access, and security for the Tent of Meeting. This tent represented the Lord's presence. The Egyptian army from around the same time period used a similar defensive formation to protect holy objects during their battle campaigns.

- Each area of the Hebrew camp had family banners, probably flags or streamers ({{Numbers 1:52|1:52}}). Modern Bedouins also use tribal symbols or battle flags. This shows the continued importance of tribe, clan, and family divisions. 

- The tribes camped around the holy place at a safe distance (compare {{Joshua 3:4|Joshua 3:4}}). This respected the distinction between God's holiness and the non-Levitical tribes.

The tribes of Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun camped in the most important spot on the east side of the Tent of Meeting. They led when Israel traveled. This largest tribal group had 186,400 people. It could protect the holy tent and its assistants very well.
The tribes of Reuben, Simeon, and Gad camped on the south. They had 151,450 soldiers and marched second in line.
The tribes of Ephraim, Manasseh, and Benjamin followed the Tent of Meeting and the Levites.
The tribes of Dan, Asher, and Naphtali were in the back.
At first, the Hebrews obeyed God's commands by camping and marching as Moses instructed. Yet, they soon stopped being obedient.

Aaron's family line provided the priests who led Israel's worship. Aaron's four sons were the core of Israel's priesthood. They served in God's presence on behalf of the people. God chose (ordained) them to lead and serve as ministers in the Tent of Meeting. They also acted as guardians of God's covenant with his people.
Israel's priests and Levites had duties like moving, assembling, protecting, and maintaining the Tent of Meeting. The way God organized the tribes highlighted his concern for these priestly tasks.

- The deaths of *Nadab and Abihu *(see {{Leviticus 10:1-2|Leviticus 10:1–2}}) showed the need to protect the holiness of the sanctuary and to strictly obey God's instructions ({{Numbers 26:61|Numbers 26:61}}; {{Leviticus 16:1|Leviticus 16:1}}; {{1 Chronicles 24:2|1 Chronicles 24:2}}; compare {{Acts 5:1-11|Acts 5:1–11}}; {{1 Corinthians 10:6-11|1 Corinthians 10:6–11}}; {{1 Corinthians 11:29-30|11:29–30}}). 

- *Eleazar and Ithamar:* See “Eleazar” Profile.

God chose the Levites to be assistants for the priests, represented by Aaron. They had a number of holy duties in their ministry service. They performed holy tasks to maintain the Tent of Meeting and its items ({{Numbers 3:7|3:7}}{{Numbers 3:8|,8}}; explained more in {{Numbers 4:1-33|4:1–33}}).
The sanctuary was set apart for God’s holy use ({{Numbers 1:51|Numbers 1:51}}; {{Numbers 3:38|3:38}}; {{Numbers 18:7|18:7}}). Only qualified people could approach it (compare {{Numbers 3:4|3:4}}).

- *every firstborn Israelite*: These belonged to God because God spared them when the Egyptian firstborn sons died ({{Numbers 3:13|3:13}}; see {{Exodus 11:1-12:51|Exodus 11–12}}). 

- *I have taken the Levites: *God chose the Levites to serve as substitutes for the firstborn sons.

- This first phase of a two-part registration of the tribe of Levi summarized each family's special duties. {{Numbers 4:1-33|4:1–33}}describes this in more detail (see {{Numbers 4:34-49|4:34–49}} for the second phase). This count did not relate to military duties, so it included male Levites from the age of one month ({{Numbers 3:40-41|3:40–41}}).

- Three family groups descend from the three sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. These clans, often called the Gershonites, Kohathites, and Merarites, later inherited the "cities of refuge" ({{Joshua 21:1-45|Joshua 21}}). They also had various important roles in the Jerusalem temple ({{2 Chronicles 29:3-17|2 Chronicles 29:3–17}}).

Aaron and Moses, sons of Amram, were descendants of Kohath (see {{Exodus 6:18|Exodus 6:18}}, {{Exodus 6:20|20}}, {{Exodus 6:26|26}}). They were caretakers of the Most Holy Place and its very holy furnishings (described in {{Numbers 3:1-4:49|Numbers 3–4}}). The Kohathites were the most respected of the three clans.
*8,600:* Some ancient Greek versions say *8,300*. The “six” (Hebrew shsh) in 8,600 could result from misreading a “three” (Hebrew shlsh).

Aaron’s third son, Eleazar, led the Levites as an administrator. He was like an executive secretary, while his father did other tasks. He had "oversight of the entire tabernacle" ({{Numbers 4:16-20|4:16–20}}). Eleazar had a key role during Israel’s time in the wilderness. He later became the high priest after his father (see {{Numbers 16:37-39|16:37–39}}; {{Numbers 19:3-6|19:3–6}}; {{Numbers 20:25-28|20:25–28}}; {{Numbers 26:1-3|26:1–3}}).
The best campsite east of the tabernacle was for Moses, Aaron, and Aaron’s sons.
*22,000:* The numbers for each clan totaled 22,300 ({{Numbers 3:22|3:22}}, {{Numbers 3:28|28}}, {{Numbers 3:34|34}}). See the study note on 3:28.

There were 273 more firstborn sons in Israel from the non-Levite tribes than there were Levite males (compare {{Numbers 3:39|Leviticus 3:39}}). The Levites acted as substitutes for Israel's firstborn sons ({{Numbers 3:41|3:41}}; see study note on 3:11–13). The law required a redemption price of five pieces of silver for each extra firstborn son ({{Numbers 3:46-48|Numbers 3:46–48}}; compare {{Leviticus 27:6|Leviticus 27:6}}). 

It is unclear who paid this cost. This arrangement for special substitutes points to Christ’s role as a substitute. Through his death, Christ paid the redemption price for all humanity (see {{Mark 10:45|Mark 10:45}}; {{Galatians 3:13|Galatians 3:13}}; {{Ephesians 1:7|Ephesians 1:7}}; {{Hebrews 9:15|Hebrews 9:15}}).
Moses and Aaron communicated God's will about the care and transport of the Tent of Meeting. This was the main duty of the three Levitical families.

- This section continues the discussion from {{Numbers 3:21-37|3:21–37}} about the duties of the three Levite clans. The Levites carried and cared for the Tent of Meeting while traveling and camping. Other tribes always surrounded them to protect them and their valuable cargo ({{Numbers 2:17|2:17}}). They placed the holy items of God in the center of the tribes. The priests and their Levitical assistants kept these items holy by separating them. 

- God, in his holiness, deserves to have the details of his will given careful attention. The Tent of Meeting and its furnishings were holy. The tribe of Levi had to maintain the difference between holy and common, and between ceremonially clean and unclean. This is why there is so much information about the duties of the three Levite clans.

Out of the 22,000 Levites, only men aged thirty to fifty could serve in the sanctuary ({{Numbers 3:39|3:39}}). This was because they were most capable at this time of their lives. {{Numbers 4:34-49|4:34–49}} lists 8,580 qualified males. This is the summary of this registration, another "numbering."

The duties of the Kohathites come first because they handled the most holy objects (see {{Numbers 3:27-32|3:27–32}}). This might be because Aaron and the priests came from this clan ({{1 Chronicles 6:2-3|1 Chronicles 6:2–3}}). Their tasks included carrying, setting up, and folding up these holy and very important coverings and furnishings. 

The items entrusted to Kohath's descendants were very valuable. These included: 

- the ark of the Testimony, 

- the table of the Bread of the Presence, 

- the lampstand (Hebrew *menorah*), 

- the gold incense altar, and 

- the altar for sacrifices. 

{{Exodus 25:1-30:38|Exodus 25–30}}first describes these objects. But Numbers shows how the Hebrews used them in daily life. The Kohathites carried these items on poles or in frames. They could not touch them or enter the sanctuary to look at them, or they would die.

Aaron and his sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, had to fully cover the sanctuary and all holy items before the camp could move. Non-Levitical tribes marched in front and behind the Levites, who carried the Tent of Meeting. The colors of the coverings showed the royalty of the objects. 

They were so holy that even the Kohathites, whom God chose to handle them, could not touch the holy items, or they would die. This respect showed the holiness of Israel's Lord. Ignoring these rules was dangerous, as shown in {{1 Samuel 6:19-20|1 Samuel 6:19–20}} and {{2 Samuel 6:6-7|2 Samuel 6:6–7}}.

The men of the Gershonite clan (see {{Numbers 3:21-26|3:21–26}}) were responsible for general service and carrying loads ({{Numbers 4:24|4:24}}). They handled the curtains, coverings, ropes, and related equipment. These were less central to Israel's worship. The duties of the Gershonites focused on the Tent of Meeting in general. This was unlike the Kohathites, who were responsible for the holy objects of the inner place of worship.

This assignment to the Merarite clan involved items of lower priority than those of the Kohathites and Gershonites. It had to be done in a specific way, with each man's load assigned by name ({{Numbers 4:32|4:32}}; see also {{1 Corinthians 14:40|1 Corinthians 14:40}}). The Gershonites and Merarites did not have the status of Kohath’s family. Yet, each group helped move and set up the Tent of Meeting.
The numbering and recording the Levites' names and ensuring each man understood his task was crucial. This helped properly organize Israel for travel and camping and protected the Tent of Meeting.

- Modern Western people may find it difficult to understand the Old Testament laws of purity. Today, things like skin diseases, bodily discharges, or contact with a dead body are viewed mainly as health concerns. But in the Old Testament, the main concern was protecting God’s holiness from ceremonial uncleanness (see {{Leviticus 11:1-15:33|Leviticus 11–15}}). 

The community had to keep the camp holy. Nothing unclean could touch what belonged to the Lord ({{Numbers 5:2-3|Numbers 5:2–3}}). They had to choose between having God in the camp or allowing a ceremonially polluted person stay. Both could not remain ({{Numbers 5:3|5:3}}). 

- The importance of purity continues from Leviticus and Numbers to the book of Revelation. Nothing ceremonially unclean will enter the New Jerusalem where God lives (see study note on Revelation 21:27). In the New Testament, impurity most often refers to what is morally impure ({{Acts 10:28|Acts 10:28}}; {{Ephesians 5:5|Ephesians 5:5}}; {{1 Thessalonians 2:3|1 Thessalonians 2:3}}; {{1 Thessalonians 4:7|4:7}}).
These laws speak about cleanliness, repayment, and staying faithful in marriage.

These legal matters were meant to protect the purity of the Israelites, their priests, and the tabernacle. Purity here refers to being clean and set apart for worship.

These rules helped the people remember who they were. Israel was a theocracy (a nation ruled directly by God). God was their true king.

Moses served as God’s main spokesman. Through him, God gave laws and instructions to the people.

- *skin disease:* The Hebrew word here describes various, contagious skin diseases (compare {{Leviticus 13:1-14:57|Leviticus 13–14}}). 

- *bodily discharge*: This refers to fluids associated with sexual organs ({{Leviticus 15:1-33|Leviticus 15}}; compare {{Luke 8:43-48|Luke 8:43–48}}). 

- *a dead person:* See {{Numbers 6:6-11|Numbers 6:6–11}}; {{Numbers 19:11|19:11}}.

The laws about confession and restitution show the strong Hebrew concern for moral behavior ({{Leviticus 6:1-7|Leviticus 6:1–7}}).

Confession means admitting one’s sin before God. Restitution means making things right by repaying what was taken or damaged. A person who wronged another had to return what was stolen and often add more as a penalty.

The Israelites were to be held responsible for their actions and their words. It was a serious matter when someone did something wrong to someone else. They had to pay the person they sinned against back and pay extra.

God explained that sinning against others hurt the relationship between the person who sinned and God. It showed that the person wasn’t being faithful to God. Their relationship with God was healed when they repented and turned away from their sin. They sacrificed a ram to show that they had repented. The death of the ram atoned for their sin. This means that it paid for the person’s sin.

Another serious matter was when husbands and wives weren’t faithful to one another. It was as important for men to be faithful as it was for women to be faithful. There were times when it was hard to know if someone had been unfaithful. Women were often falsely accused of being unfaithful. So God provided a way for women to show that they weren’t guilty. This practice wasn’t magic. It showed that God would bring judgement against those who weren’t faithful in marriage.

It was also a serious matter when people made a promise to God. This was clear in the instructions about being a Nazirite. The words of the priests to the people were another serious matter. God commanded them to speak words of blessing. The priests’ words would help the Israelites trust that God was with them. God wanted them to trust that he cared for them and provided peace for them.

Harming another person is also betraying the Lord (literally *to act unfaithful in unfaithfulness*; compare {{Numbers 5:8|Leviticus 5:8}}). Being right with God leads to being right with others. If we treat others wrongly, it shows our relationship with the Lord is not right.
This restitution and the guilt offering for the sin were intended to teach personal responsibility to live holy with God (see {{Leviticus 6:1-7:38|Leviticus 6–7}}).

- Since sin is ultimately against God, the one doing wrong must make restitution to the *LORD* ({{Numbers 5:6|Leviticus 5:6}}; {{Psalm 51:4|Psalm 51:4}}). God allowed the human victims of the sin to receive this payment. If no victims were alive, the priest would receive the payment on behalf of the LORD. Those doing wrong must also offer a valuable sacrifice to restore their ceremonial purity and their relationship with God ({{Numbers 5:1-4|Numbers 5:1–4}}). 

- *the atonement is made for him:* See study note on Leviticus 1:4.

Priests partially supported their families by receiving a share of the sacrifices. Sometimes, they could sell extra sacrifices to fund the priesthood, maintain the sanctuary, and help with other religious needs (see {{1 Corinthians 8:4-13|1 Corinthians 8:4–13}}).

This detailed test for adultery, a "trial by ordeal," is the only one in the Old Testament. Yet, trial by ordeal was common in the ancient Near East. God had a special interest in protecting marriage. It was the foundation of Hebrew society. 

The ordeal was intended to promote marital faithfulness. We do not know how often such ordeals actually happened. This procedure relied on God to intervene so that justice occurred when evidence was lacking (see {{1 Corinthians 5:5|1 Corinthians 5:5}}).
The husband presented his case to the priest, and the “law of jealousy” ({{Numbers 5:29|5:29}}) transferred the husband's jealousy and suspicion to a higher court of appeal.
The holy water and the dust were sacred because of their association with the sanctuary.

*making your thigh shrivel and your belly swell: Thigh* is a polite way to speak about the reproductive organs (compare {{Genesis 24:2|Genesis 24:2}}; {{Genesis 47:29|47:29}}). Something would stop her ability to have children. The punishment matched the crime, as sexual immorality led to infertility.
The image of drinking curses appears again in {{Ezekiel 2:8-3:3|Ezekiel 2:8–3:3}} and {{Revelation 10:8-11|Revelation 10:8–11}}.

The law describes a trial by ordeal (a test in which God was asked to show guilt or innocence). In this case, a husband could bring his wife to the priest if he suspected adultery.

The summary of the law makes one point clear. If the husband raised questions about his wife’s guilt or innocence, he was not considered guilty simply for asking.

Some readers may notice what seems like a double standard. Ancient laws often focused on the woman’s failure in cases of adultery. This pattern was common in the ancient world.

However, Israel’s legal system did not excuse the man involved. The law required punishment for both parties in an affair (as in {{Leviticus 20:10|Leviticus 20:10}}; {{Deuteronomy 22:21-22|Deuteronomy 22:21–22}}).

The voluntary *vow of a Nazirite *allowed men or women to *separate* themselves *to the LORD*. The Nazirite lifestyle varied throughout Hebrew history. People took vows seriously in ancient times as a way to show devotion or gratitude to God. This vow could be temporary or permanent. It involved avoiding alcoholic drinks, not cutting hair, and avoiding contact with corpses. 

Nazirite restrictions allowed members of non-Levitical tribes to have a more demanding and highly respected relationship with God. The Nazirite vow is probably best known because of Samson ({{Judges 13:1-16:31|Judges 13–16}}). See also {{1 Samuel 1:11|1 Samuel 1:11}}; {{Jeremiah 35:1-19|Jeremiah 35}}; {{Acts 18:18|Acts 18:18}}; {{Acts 21:23-26|21:23–26}}; compare {{Luke 1:15|Luke 1:15}}.
*Nazirite:* The Hebrew word *nazir* comes from a verb meaning "to separate."

The law required priests to avoid drinking wine before serving in the Tent of Meeting ({{Leviticus 10:9|Leviticus 10:9}}). The Nazirite vow allowed non-Levites to extend this rule. They avoided wine everywhere, at all times, and anything from a grapevine.

*hair:* This had a special symbolic meaning (see {{Leviticus 19:27|Leviticus 19:27}}). Religious people often left their hair uncut or shaved it completely ({{Numbers 8:5-7|Numbers 8:5–7}}). The Israelites did not have to leave their hair completely uncut, but the Nazirites did.

Touching dead bodies made people ceremonially unclean ({{Numbers 9:6-10|9:6–10}}). Priests could only touch the dead bodies of close relatives ({{Leviticus 21:1-4|Leviticus 21:1–4}}). But Nazirites could not touch any dead body at all.

The law gave instructions for restoring purity after unavoidable contact with a dead body. Contact with a dead body made a person ceremonially unclean (not fit for worship for a period of time). The person had to follow certain steps in order to be restored.

Special procedures and offerings also marked the end of a Nazirite vow. A Nazirite vow was a special promise to set oneself apart for God for a period of time. When the time ended, the person brought sacrifices and completed the required rituals.

The law also gives a strong warning about fulfilling the vow ({{Numbers 6:21|6:21}}). A person who made such a promise had to complete it fully. God expected faithfulness in keeping vows made to him.

The priestly blessing connects to the themes of worship and purity in chapters {{Numbers 5:1-6:27|5–6}}. It is a prayer where priests ask for God's blessings for Israel. As representatives of God, priests had the duty to pray (compare {{Leviticus 9:23|Leviticus 9:23}}; {{Deuteronomy 10:8|Deuteronomy 10:8}}). This prayer is similar to the high priestly prayer of Jesus in {{John 17:1-26|John 17}}.

The first half of this verse asks for blessings like health, wealth, and fertility. 

The second half seeks protection from all kinds of dangers. This prayer is similar to the language in {{Psalm 121:3-8|Psalms 121:3–8}}; {{Psalm 140:4|140:4}}; {{Psalm 141:9|and 141:9}}. These sincere requests are still good examples for prayer and blessings that people can seek for everyone. The entire poem emphasizes the Lord as the source of all good things.

{{Psalm 67:1|Psalm 67:1}} has a short version of this blessing. This is similar to one found on a silver amulet from Ketef Hinnom, southwest of Jerusalem’s Old City. A second, larger silver amulet from the same tomb has the full blessing with words almost the same as here. 

The Second Temple period lasted from Ezra to the time of Jesus. Priests would give a blessing at each day's sacrifice or at the end of services. This blessing is still used in Jewish and Christian liturgy (the formal order of prayers and worship, as in {{Numbers 6:27|6:27}}).

- *may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you*: This is a desire for God's approval. 

- *be gracious to you:* God's people need his grace and mercy in a dangerous world (compare {{Psalm 31:16|Psalms 31:16}}; {{Psalm 67:1|67:1}}; {{Psalm 80:3|80:3}}, {{Psalm 80:7|7}}, {{Psalm 80:19|19}}).

God's favor, shown through his countenance or face, means his approval and special attention (compare {{Psalm 30:7|Psalm 30:7}}). Divine peace (Hebrew *shalom*) is more than only the absence of conflict or violence. God's peace brings complete well-being, health, and wholeness.

The priests were mediators of God’s covenant with Israel. A mediator is someone who stands between two parties to represent them. The priests stood between God and the people.

Their duty was to pray for the people. They also spoke God’s blessing over them. In this way, they helped maintain the covenant relationship between God and Israel (see {{Romans 8:34|Romans 8:34}}; {{Hebrews 2:17-18|Hebrews 2:17–18}}; {{Hebrews 4:14-16|4:14–16}}). He intercedes for believers, which means he prays for them before God. As the great high priest, he brings his people into God’s presence and secures God’s blessing for them.

- Moses set up the tabernacle on the first day of the second year after the exodus from Egypt ({{Exodus 40:1-2|Exodus 40:1–2}}). 

- Moses finished setting up the tabernacle. Then *he anointed and consecrated it and all its furnishings, along with the altar and all its utensils* (compare {{Exodus 40:9-10|Exodus 40:9–10}}; {{Leviticus 8:10-11|Leviticus 8:10–11}}). The altar, as the place of sacrifice, was especially important among the holy furniture.
This is a detailed description of the offerings made by Israel's 12 tribes during the dedication of the tabernacle. They dedicated these gifts for 12 days.

Exodus chapters 35 to 39 described how the Israelites built the holy tent. They obeyed God’s instructions about the tent completely.

But before the tent could be used to worship God, many supplies were needed. Numbers recorded how the Israelites obeyed God completely in gathering these supplies.

Leaders from all the tribes except Levi brought the same amount of supplies. This showed that all the tribes were important no matter how big or small they were.

The Levites didn’t bring supplies. The Levites themselves were an offering to God. Levite males had work to do in the holy tent. They did this work from the age of 25 until 50.

Once the holy tent was set up, God started speaking to Moses there. Moses heard God’s voice from above the ark of the covenant. The cloud that covered the tent showed that God was present there.

- The same tribal leaders who helped with the registration in chapter {{Numbers 1:1-54|1}}also appear in {{Numbers 7:2-3|7:2–3}}. The non-Levitical tribes gave the Gershonites and Merarites wagons and oxen to move the heavy parts of the tabernacle and other items (see chapter {{Numbers 4:1-49|4}}). 

- These vehicles and animals were the first offerings from the Hebrew tribes ({{Numbers 7:2|7:2}}). The tribal leaders also presented these practical gifts along with the more elaborate offerings they dedicated ({{Numbers 7:10|7:10}}, {{Numbers 7:12-83|12–83}}).

Later, the Israelites tried to move the ark of the covenant using a cart, but it ended tragically ({{1 Samuel 6:8|1 Samuel 6:8}}, {{1 Samuel 6:11|11}}; {{2 Samuel 6:3|2 Samuel 6:3}}, {{2 Samuel 6:6-7|6–7}}).

When they anointed the altar, the tribal leaders gave the wagons and oxen, silver and gold vessels, and other religious offerings for the altar. Starting with the tribe of Judah, the leaders brought these gifts to the tabernacle for 12 days. They collected these gifts from the Egyptians when Israel left Egypt (compare {{Exodus 12:35-36|Exodus 12:35–36}}; {{Exodus 25:3|25:3}}).

One by one, the tribal leaders brought their gifts for the dedication of the altar. Each tribe participated until the whole Hebrew confederation (the united group of twelve tribes) had taken part.

The text repeats the description of each tribe’s gift. This repetition highlights the shared nature of the ceremony. Every tribe had a role in setting apart their place of worship for God.

The careful listing of the gifts may reflect detailed record keeping, like an archive or ledger (an official written record). The text notes that the silver bowls and plates contained grain offerings. The gold dishes held incense.

Each tribe also brought animals for a burnt offering, a sin offering, and a peace offering, as required in Leviticus. These offerings showed worship, repentance, and fellowship with God.

This paragraph first summarizes the gifts and offerings from each tribe. Then it lists expensive containers, offerings, incense, and sacrificial animals. These large and costly gifts showed the importance of the altar, the tabernacle, and the God who was served there. The law required these sacrifices, but the Hebrews gave the special gifts generously.

- After dedicating the Tent of Meeting (the tabernacle) and setting it apart as holy, it became the center of divine revelation. There, Moses spoke with God, who revealed his will and presence ({{Leviticus 16:2|Leviticus 16:2}}, {{Leviticus 16:13-17|13–17}}). This communication came from the ark of the covenant. It was specifically between the two cherubim above the ark's cover, also called "the mercy seat" (compare {{Exodus 25:17-22|Exodus 25:17–22}}). 

- For the Israelites, this was the special place for atonement, similar to the significance in the Christian faith of the cross where Jesus died (see {{Hebrews 9:1-10:39|Hebrews 9–10}}, especially {{Hebrews 9:5|Hebrews 9:5}}). God's voice, heard by Moses the mediator, fulfilled the promise in {{Exodus 25:22|Exodus 25:22}} and {{Numbers 30:6|Numbers 30:6}}. The Lord's presence ensured the holiness of Israel's wilderness place of worship.

These verses give specific instructions for placing the lampstand (Hebrew *menorah*) in the tabernacle. The lampstand (see {{Exodus 25:31-40|Exodus 25:31–40}}). It was made with branches shaped like a stylized tree.

The inside of the tabernacle had no windows, so it was dark. The light from the lampstand helped the priests carry out their duties.
The Lord gave instructions for the dedication and cleansing of the Levites. The Levites were set apart to serve in the tabernacle.

- The ceremony to make the Levites ceremonially clean involved sprinkling with water, shaving all hair, and wearing clean clothes. This was similar to ceremonies for cleansing from ceremonial impurity. 

- *water of purification:* This phrase appears only here. The sprinkling symbolized washing away sin and had symbolic importance similar to later Jewish washings and Christian baptism. This water might have been the same as the mixture with ashes from the red heifer that removed sin (see {{Numbers 19:9|19:9}}; also {{Hebrews 9:13|Hebrews 9:13}}). 

- Shaving their entire body was also part of being declared ceremonially clean from the ceremonial impurity of polluting diseases ({{Leviticus 14:8|Leviticus 14:8}}). 

- Washing clothes was part of all cleansing from ceremonial impurity (for example, {{Leviticus 15:5-27|Leviticus 15:5–27}}).
*laying their hands on them: *Israel acknowledged the Levites' special status and offered them as their representatives in the presence of the Lord ({{Numbers 8:16|8:16}}).

The mention of Aaron's raised hands suggests that Israel offered the Levites to the Lord as a *wave offering*. Priests would lift up this type of offering to the Lord (compare {{Leviticus 7:30|Leviticus 7:30}}). The Levites committed themselves to tasks that made them living and holy sacrifices (compare {{Romans 12:1|Romans 12:1}}).
The Levites offered the right sacrifices before doing their work in the Tent of Meeting ({{Numbers 8:15|8:15}}).
A plague was an appropriate punishment for unlawful actions ({{Numbers 11:33|11:33}}; {{Numbers 14:37|14:37}}).

- These are guidelines for the length of the Levites' service. 

- Whereas {{Numbers 4:3|4:3}} says their service in the Tent of Meeting started at age 30, {{Numbers 8:24|8:24}} says age 25. This difference might show changes in age requirements over time, depending on how many Levite men were available. Those aged 25–29 might have been unofficial workers or apprentices. 

- Both passages set the retirement age at 50. Retired Levites could serve as guards of the Tent of Meeting (see {{Psalm 84:10|Psalm 84:10}}).
A year after Israel left Egypt, it was time for them to celebrate their second Passover in the Sinai wilderness. Those unable to celebrate at the set time could do so a month later.

Priests were to blow the silver trumpets to give messages to the Israelites.

God said that the sound would remind him of the Israelites. This didn’t mean that God sometimes forgot about them. This was a way of describing how much attention God pays to his people (God’s people). He always takes care of them. He even listens to the noises they make.

Before leaving the desert around Mount Sinai, the Israelites celebrated the Passover Feast again.

Outsiders like Hobab could participate in the feast (feasts) if they wanted to.

Then the tribes marched away from Sinai. They obeyed God completely by leaving the camp in the order God had told them to. The sign to do this was when the cloud over the holy tent moved.

- God told the Hebrews to celebrate Passover at the set time (see {{Exodus 12:6|Exodus 12:6}}). 

- *at twilight:* The Hebrew day starts at sunset.
When it was time to celebrate Passover, some men could not participate due to the rules in {{Leviticus 7:20-21|Leviticus 7:20–21}}. They wanted to follow the rules, but it seemed impossible for them.
Moses agreed to ask the Lord about this difficult case (compare {{Numbers 7:89|7:89}}).

God's solution to the problem was to allow a makeup ceremony one month later for two special cases (see also {{2 Chronicles 30:1-27|2 Chronicles 30}}). Yet, he warned the Israelites not to neglect the Passover and to celebrate it according to the rules.

The Israelites could not break the bones of the Passover lamb (see {{Exodus 12:46|Exodus 12:46}}; {{Psalm 34:20|Psalm 34:20}}; {{John 19:32-36|John 19:32–36}}; compare {{John 1:29|John 1:29}}; {{1 Corinthians 5:7|1 Corinthians 5:7}}). The apostle John mentioned this instruction when he wrote that they did not break the legs of Jesus when he was on the cross ({{John 19:36|John 19:36}}).

If a person refused to observe the required Passover, that person was to be cut off from the community. The Passover was a central act of worship that remembered God’s rescue of Israel from Egypt.

The phrase “cut off” can have more than one meaning in the Old Testament. It may refer to the death penalty. It may also mean banishment from the community (being removed from the people). The exact meaning in this case is not fully clear (see study note on Leviticus 7:20–21).

Foreigners who lived among the Hebrews and wanted to celebrate the Passover could do so by following the same laws, but circumcision was required for males who desired to eat the Passover meal (see also {{Exodus 12:48-49|Exodus 12:48–49}}).

This passage is similar to {{Exodus 40:17|Exodus 40:17}}, {{Exodus 40:34-38|34–38}}. It gives more details about how God used the pillar of cloud and fire to lead his people (see also {{Exodus 13:21-22|Exodus 13:21–22}}). The Lord was faithful and clearly guided his people in the wilderness.
Even Israel's enemies saw the fiery cloud ({{Numbers 14:14|14:14}}). This clearly represented God's glorious presence and the way he guided their movement.

- Israel needed clear signals so the tribes could receive instructions. Two silver trumpets provided a simple and effective way to signal all the tribes to move. 

- These trumpets were not the ram’s horns (Hebrew *shofar*) often mentioned in the Old Testament (for example, {{Joshua 6:4-6|Joshua 6:4–6}}). Israelite craftsmen made them from hammered silver brought out of Egypt.
They used the two trumpets to alert people for important announcements (compare {{Revelation 8:1-11:19|Revelation 8–11}}).

When it was time to journey to the next destination, the trumpets sounded to signal when to camp and when to move. This sound was in addition to the movement of the pillar of cloud (compare {{Numbers 9:15-22|9:15–22}} and chapter {{Numbers 2:1-34|2}}).
*the priests, are to sound the trumpets: *They used these trumpets only for matters related to God and his rule over Israel, which the priests served.

The trumpets marked holy events that people might not easily recognize. Trumpets that called to battle would remind the Lord to save the Hebrews from their enemies ({{Hosea 5:8|Hosea 5:8}}; {{Joel 2:1|Joel 2:1}}).

Leaving Sinai was a key moment in Israel's history. The Israelites now had the law and God would test them on how they obeyed it. The departure from Sinai marked the start of the march toward Canaan, although it became a long journey (compare {{Deuteronomy 1:6-8|Deuteronomy 1:6–8}}, {{Deuteronomy 1:19|19}}). This passage summarizes the daily routines during the journey.

The Israelites traveled to the wilderness of Paran. This region was dry and harsh. It was either arid or semi-arid, which means it received very little rain.

The wilderness of Paran lay in the northeastern part of the Sinai Peninsula. It was south of the Negev and west of the Dead Sea and the Arabah Rift (a long valley that runs from the Dead Sea southward; compare {{Genesis 21:21|Genesis 21:21}}).

The order of march described here is different from {{Numbers 2:3-34|2:3–34}}. There, all three Levitical clans carried the tabernacle and its furnishings in the center of the camp. They marched between the groups led by Judah and Reuben, and the groups led by Ephraim and Dan.

In this passage, the arrangement is more detailed. The Gershonites and Merarites carried the structural parts of the tabernacle between Judah and Reuben. The Kohathites carried the most sacred furniture between Reuben and Ephraim.

This arrangement was practical. It gave the Gershonites and Merarites time to set up the tabernacle before the Kohathites arrived with the sacred objects. This plan also provided protection for the holy items.

In addition, this pattern spread the Levites among the tribes. Their presence among the people may have strengthened spiritual influence throughout the camp (compare {{Matthew 13:33|Matthew 13:33}}; {{Matthew 16:6|16:6}}, {{Matthew 16:11-12|11–12}}; {{1 Corinthians 5:6-7|1 Corinthians 5:6–7}}).

- After the journey toward Paran began, Moses asked his brother-in-law, Hobab, to guide the Israelites (literally *and you will serve for us for eyes*) (compare {{Judges 4:11|Judges 4:11}}). In this way, Hobab would share in their promised blessings. As a Midianite shepherd, Hobab knew the routes and possible sources of food and water in the Sinai Peninsula. 

- *Reuel the Midianite:* See “Jethro (Reuel)” Profile. 

- *my own land and my own people: *Midian was probably in northwestern Arabia. {{Judges 1:16|Judges 1:16}} suggests that Hobab accepted the request.

*the mountain of the LORD:* Here, this refers to Mount Sinai. In other places, it means Mount Moriah or Zion in Jerusalem ({{Genesis 22:14|Genesis 22:14}}; {{Psalm 24:3|Psalm 24:3}}; {{Isaiah 2:3|Isaiah 2:3}}; {{Zechariah 8:3|Zechariah 8:3}}).

When the ark of the covenant set out, Moses called on the Lord as a warrior. He acknowledged the Lord would help Israel win the promised land and fight their battles (compare {{Psalm 68:1|Psalm 68:1}}).
This invocation (formal call for God’s help) asked the Lord to be present with his people. It was spoken when the Israelites set out or camped.

- *Soon the people began to complain … fire from the LORD blazed:* The link between Israel’s complaints and God’s punishment is a major theme in Numbers and throughout the Old Testament (for example, {{Deuteronomy 9:22|Deuteronomy 9:22}}; {{Psalm 78:1-72|Psalm 78}}). God is holy and just, and he demands obedience from his people. Complaints are the same as rejecting him (compare {{Numbers 11:20|Numbers 11:20}}). 

- *their hardship:* Mount Sinai had been a stable home for a year. The journey to Paran brought heat, thirst, and fatigue. 

- *consumed the outskirts of the camp: *Compare {{Leviticus 10:2|Leviticus 10:2}}.
This is one of many occasions in the wilderness when Israel was disobedient to the Lord.

Many of the Israelites spoke against God and didn’t obey him. They complained about how hard life was and about their food. They complained about Moses as their leader. Even Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses.

The complaining showed that God’s people didn’t want God to be their God. They wished that God hadn’t saved them from being slaves in Egypt. They didn’t accept the ways that God had saved them and provided for them.

God brought judgement against them for refusing to accept him. He sent a fire, plague and disease among the Israelites. Yet God didn’t destroy all of them. He was patient with his people and forgave them.

God shared the power of the Holy Spirit with 70 leaders. He did this so that they could help Moses. But God made something clear about Moses. Moses was close to him like no other human being was.

Moses sent 12 spies to look at the land of Canaan. Of the 12, only Joshua and Caleb urged the people to obey God. But the Israelites refused to enter Canaan. That happened at Kadesh Barnea.

This meant that they were saying no to who God is. They were saying no to God’s covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

As a result the Israelites would wander for 40 years in the desert. They would wander until those who had refused to enter Canaan died. After that, their children would receive the covenant blessing of the land.

- The people asked Moses to speak to God again on their behalf. This stopped the fire of God's judgment (compare {{Exodus 15:25|Exodus 15:25}}; {{Exodus 32:11-14|32:11–14}}). 

- *Taberah:* Compare {{Numbers 11:34-35|Numbers 11:34–35}}; see {{Deuteronomy 9:22|Deuteronomy 9:22}}.

*Who will feed us meat?:* The Israelites had flocks and herds (for example, {{Numbers 32:1|32:1}}; {{Exodus 12:32|Exodus 12:32}}, {{Exodus 12:38|38}}; {{Exodus 17:3|17:3}}; {{Exodus 34:3|34:3}}). But the animals were more valuable for their dairy products and other benefits while alive. They only butchered them for meat occasionally. The Hebrews did not have enough meat to regularly feed such a large population (compare {{Numbers 11:21-22|Numbers 11:21–22}}).

Israel had not given up the attitude that led to judgment at Taberah ({{Numbers 11:1-3|11:1–3}}). At Taberah, the people complained, and the Lord sent fire among them.

Soon after, they joined the foreign rabble (a mixed group of non-Israelites who had left Egypt with them) in craving the foods of Egypt. They longed for the fish, vegetables, and other foods they had known there.

In doing this, they forgot the suffering and slavery they had experienced in Egypt. They remembered the food but ignored the hardship.
The Lord had earlier provided manna and quail ({{Exodus 16:1-36|Exodus 16}}).
People often explain *manna* as a naturally occurring edible substance (but see {{Deuteronomy 8:3|Deuteronomy 8:3}}). Yet, its amount and how long it lasted was miraculous.

- The Israelites' constant complaining frustrated Moses, leading him to express his own complaints to God. With extreme sarcasm, Moses reminded God that he had not wanted this responsibility (compare {{Exodus 4:10|Exodus 4:10}}). Israel became such a burden that Moses wished God would do him the favor of ending his life (compare {{Job 6:9|Job 6:9}}). 

- Moses' complaint was acceptable, unlike the people's complaints, because he sought the Lord instead of longing for Egypt's pleasures.

Jethro suggested that Moses should have different levels of judges ({{Exodus 18:13-26|Exodus 18:13–26}}). He focused on practical issues like the tribal leaders who helped Moses with the registration ({{Numbers 1:5-15|Numbers 1:5–15}}). 

In contrast, the group of 70 elders would give Israel spiritual guidance. They needed a share of God's Spirit. Moses already had this, and it made him the Lord's special spokesman. Their ability to lead depended on God's Spirit being with them (compare {{1 Samuel 10:6|1 Samuel 10:6}}; {{1 Samuel 19:20|19:20}}; {{Joel 2:28|Joel 2:28}}; {{Acts 2:16-18|Acts 2:16–18}}; {{1 Corinthians 12:10|1 Corinthians 12:10}}; {{2 Peter 1:20-21|2 Peter 1:20–21}}).

The text does not describe what happened when the Spirit rested on them and they prophesied. It only says that they spoke as the Spirit enabled them.

Whatever took place, it may have included ecstatic speech (intense or Spirit-driven words spoken in a special way). Similar events appear later in {{Acts 2:4|Acts 2:4}} and {{1 Corinthians 14:2|1 Corinthians 14:2}}. However, the text suggests that this was a unique event.

Joshua’s worthy jealousy was a desire to safeguard his master’s status. But, Moses was humble and did not feel threatened by Eldad and Medad's prophecy ({{Numbers 12:3|Numbers 12:3}}). Instead, he was glad to see God working through others in special ways. Moses had leadership qualities that the younger Joshua had not yet developed (compare {{Mark 9:38-40|Mark 9:38–40}}).

God answered the people's complaints by sending a storm of quail and a plague. God had given quail with manna in {{Exodus 16:13|Exodus 16:13}}. But here the quail showed God's judgment through an excessive abundance.
The exact locations of Kibroth-hattaavah and Hazeroth are unknown.

Most interpreters believe *the Cushite woman* is Zipporah, the wife of Moses. She was from Midian ({{Exodus 2:16-22|Exodus 2:16–22}}). They see *Cush* as referring to Cushan, a region and people near Midian ({{Habakkuk 3:7|Habakkuk 3:7}}). 

Other interpreters think *Cushite* refers to Kusi in northern Arabia, Ethiopia, or Sudan. This would suggest she was a different wife. 

In either case, it is possible that Miriam and Aaron disapproved of his having married a non-Israelite or that they were jealous of her influence over Moses.

Miriam and Aaron may have seen the marriage of Moses as a threat to their status and goals. The verses list Miriam first, suggesting she started this family conflict. This could explain why God punished her and not Aaron ({{Numbers 12:9-10|12:9–10}}).

Rebellion did not come only from the “rabble” or from the Israelites who were tired of manna ({{Numbers 11:4|11:4}}). It also came from within the family of Moses.

Aaron the high priest and Miriam the prophetess spoke against Moses ({{Exodus 29:30|Exodus 29:30}}; {{Exodus 15:20|Exodus 15:20}}). Their actions showed that even Israel’s spiritual leaders struggled with jealousy and doubt.

At this time, Israel was moving toward a lowest point in its rebellion against God ({{Numbers 13:25-14:12|Numbers 13:25–14:12}}).

- Challenging the authority of Moses meant rejecting the Lord's choice of him as Israel's leader. 

- *the LORD heard this:* The same phrase in {{Numbers 11:1|11:1}} hints at the Lord's response.

- The humility of Moses stands in sharp contrast to the jealousy of Miriam and Aaron. The text says that Moses was very humble. His character reflected a godly spirit (see also {{Proverbs 3:34|Proverbs 3:34}}; {{Matthew 5:5|Matthew 5:5}}). 

- The statement about the humility of Moses appears as a parenthetical comment (a brief note inserted into the story). It presents the truth from God’s point of view.

Some think these words may have been written by Moses. Others believe they may have been added later by an editor. In either case, the comment highlights the faithful and humble character of Moses.
In response to this rebellion, the Lord spoke directly. He reaffirmed the special status and authority of Moses.

The Lord trusted Moses, leading to a close relationship. God communicated with prophets through visions and dreams, but he spoke to Moses *face to face* (literally *mouth to mouth;* see {{Exodus 33:8-11|Exodus 33:8–11}}, {{Exodus 33:18-23|18–23}}; {{Deuteronomy 34:10|Deuteronomy 34:10}}).

Miriam experienced the burning anger of the Lord (see study note on 12:1–2). When Aaron saw what happened to her, he confessed their sin and asked Moses to pray for them (compare {{Numbers 11:2|11:2}}). Both Moses and the Lord accepted Aaron's confession.
Miriam had to follow the usual steps to become ceremonially pure after a skin disease ({{Numbers 5:2-4|5:2–4}}; {{Leviticus 13:1-14:57|Leviticus 13–14}}).
The camp in the Wilderness of Paran was at Kadesh-barnea ({{Numbers 13:26|13:26}}; {{Deuteronomy 1:19-22|Deuteronomy 1:19–22}}).

Moses chose a leader from each tribe to explore the land God promised to the Hebrews. The tribes listed are from chapter {{Numbers 1:1-54|1}}, but the order is different. Caleb and Joshua later prove to be men of faith ({{Numbers 14:30|14:30}}).

Twelve spies explored the fertile land of Canaan and found strong enemies defending it. Earlier chapters show Israel's disobedience, hinting at future failures. The Israelites did not have the obedience, courage, or faith to capture the land. So, the Lord made them spend 40 years in the Wilderness of Sinai. That generation did not receive their inheritance in the promised land.

The scouting mission had a clear military purpose. The spies also needed to gather information about natural resources and food. These things were concerning to the Israelites since they left Egypt (chapter {{Numbers 11:1-35|11}}; {{Exodus 16:1-36|Exodus 16}}).
The season for harvesting the first ripe grapes came in late July or August, during the summer.

- The distance from the Wilderness of Zin to Lebo-hamath in Syria was about 275 miles. The Wilderness of Zin was between the wilderness of Paran and Canaan's southern border see {{Numbers 34:3-5|34:3–5}}; {{Joshua 15:1-4|Joshua 15:1–4}}). *Lebo-hamath* means "entrance of Hamath." This could refer to a mountain pass or a city near Hamath. 

- The exact location of Rehob is unclear. But it was probably the same as Old Testament Beth-rehob, near a major route to Hamath. This text outlines the approximate borders of the promised land (see {{1 Kings 8:65|1 Kings 8:65}}). The phrase *from Dan to Beersheba* often marked Israel’s traditional boundaries ({{Judges 20:1|Judges 20:1}}; {{2 Samuel 3:10|2 Samuel 3:10}}). It covered a smaller area than the territory explored by Israel’s spies.
The spies explored the land of Canaan. In contrast to the Sinai wilderness, it was rich and fertile.

- Israel's spies traveled into Canaan's hill country through the Negev, the dry southern region near the wilderness of Zin. In the southern part of Canaan's central hill country, they reached Hebron. This was where Israel's ancestors had lived ({{Genesis 13:18|Genesis 13:18}}; {{Genesis 23:19|23:19}}; {{Genesis 35:27|35:27}}; {{Genesis 37:14|37:14}}). 

- The descendants of Anak were famous for their size and strength (for example, {{Deuteronomy 9:2|Deuteronomy 9:2}}). 

- *Zoan* (later called *Tanis* by the Greeks) was a famous city in Egypt's eastern delta (see also {{Psalm 78:12|Psalms 78:12}}, {{Psalm 78:43|43}}; {{Isaiah 19:11-13|Isaiah 19:11–13}}; {{Isaiah 30:3-5|30:3–5}}).
The spies agreed the land was good, but most doubted Israel could conquer it. The strong and well-fed Canaanites had built fortified towns for protection.

Kadesh is often linked to ‘Ain el-Qudeirat, a spring at the northern border of Sinai and the southern edge of Canaan. There is no evidence of a Hebrew camp there during the exodus or the wilderness wanderings. So, some scholars have suggested that ancient Kadesh was in a different location.

The promised land is also known as land *flowing with milk and honey*. In biblical times, *milk* and dairy were key parts of the diet. *Milk* symbolized abundance (see {{Deuteronomy 32:14|Deuteronomy 32:14}}; {{Isaiah 55:1|Isaiah 55:1}}; {{Joel 3:18|Joel 3:18}}). *Honey* added sweetness (see {{Psalm 19:10|Psalms 19:10}}; {{Psalm 119:103|119:103}}; {{Ezekiel 3:3|Ezekiel 3:3}}; {{Revelation 10:9-10|Revelation 10:9–10}}). The phrase describes a desirable place with plenty of food and resources (compare {{Numbers 16:13-14|Numbers 16:13–14}}; see also {{Exodus 3:8|Exodus 3:8}}; {{Deuteronomy 6:3|Deuteronomy 6:3}}; {{Deuteronomy 26:15|26:15}}; {{Jeremiah 11:4-5|Jeremiah 11:4–5}}; {{Ezekiel 20:6|Ezekiel 20:6}}). 

The New Testament emphasizes the spiritual nature of God's promises, pointing to a promised inheritance in heaven (see {{Romans 9:6-8|Romans 9:6–8}}; {{Galatians 6:14-16|Galatians 6:14–16}}; {{Revelation 21:1-2|Revelation 21:1–2}}).
The spies answer the question of {{Numbers 13:18|13:18}}. Many ethnic groups lived in ancient Canaan.
Caleb and Joshua (see {{Numbers 14:6|14:6}}, {{Numbers 14:10|10}}, {{Numbers 14:30|30}}) gave a more positive report about the land than the other spies did (compare {{Numbers 14:31-33|14:31–33}}).
*Nephilim:* See the study note on Genesis 6:4.

The people rejected the testimony of the faithful spies, Joshua and Caleb. Then rebellion spread throughout the community. Moses intervened to save Israel from total destruction. Those who disobeyed God died during a 40-year journey in the wilderness.

- The threats they complained about were real, but the Israelites should have trusted the Lord. In the ancient Near East, victors often took wives and children as plunder after battles. 

- *go back to Egypt:* The Israelites quickly forgot their slavery and the difficulties of the wilderness ({{Exodus 2:23-24|Exodus 2:23–24}}; {{Numbers 11:1|Numbers 11:1}}).
Moses and Aaron bowed down to show humility, fear, grief, and anguish.
Joshua and Caleb tried to stop the rebellion and prevent God's punishment. They tore their clothing to show their sorrow.

- Joshua and Caleb realized that Israel's lack of courage and criticism of Moses and Aaron were acts of rebellion against the Lord. They knew the consequences of this rebellion. 

- *the LORD is with us:* This was the source of their confidence (compare {{Romans 8:31|Romans 8:31}}).

*Joshua and Caleb* encouraged trust in God, which led to more opposition. The protests against the leaders turned into threats against the faithful spies. All the Israelites' objections stopped suddenly. This was because *the glory *(Hebrew *kabod*) *of the LORD* appeared at the Tent of Meeting, the site of divine communication (see {{Exodus 24:15-18|Exodus 24:15–18}}; {{Ezekiel 1:1-28|Ezekiel 1}}) .

God seemed amazed that Israel still did not trust him. This was despite his miraculous rescue from slavery and provision for their needs in the wilderness (see {{Deuteronomy 4:32-40|Deuteronomy 4:32–40}}; {{Matthew 11:21|Matthew 11:21}}; {{Luke 10:13|Luke 10:13}}).

God is patient, but he will not tolerate open rebellion from his people (see {{Exodus 32:7-10|Exodus 32:7–10}}). 

In the New Testament, the writer of Hebrews mentions this event to strengthen the faith of Christians whose trust in the gospel was weakening ({{Hebrews 3:7-19|Hebrews 3:7–19}}; {{Hebrews 12:3|12:3}}, {{Hebrews 12:25|25}}; see also {{Psalm 95:8-11|Psalm 95:8–11}}).
Moses spoke to God on behalf of his people. He reminded God that his reputation related to Israel's. He pleaded for God to continue his faithfulness.

Moses had used this argument before when he asked for forgiveness for Israel's rebellion ({{Exodus 32:10-14|Exodus 32:10–14}}). Moses knew God would still punish the Israelites ({{Deuteronomy 7:9-10|Deuteronomy 7:9–10}}).

Since leaving Egypt, Israel’s history had been marked by repeated transgressions (acts of disobedience; chapters {{Numbers 11:1-12:16|11–12}}; {{Exodus 15:22-27|Exodus 15:22–27}}; {{Exodus 17:1-7|17:1–7}}; {{Exodus 32:1-14|32:1–14}}; {{Leviticus 10:1-20|Leviticus 10}}).
Because Moses argued with God, God forgave Israel's rebellion and did not destroy them. Yet, the stubborn generation of adults would never see the promised land.

The people did not obey or have faith because they refused to listen to God's voice. They had seen the Lord's glory and miraculous signs (see study note on 14:10; {{Exodus 4:29-31|Exodus 4:29–31}}; {{Exodus 7:1-11:10|7:1–11:10}}; {{Exodus 14:15-31|14:15–31}}; {{Exodus 16:1-17:13|16:1–17:13}}).

- After leaving the promised land, God told the Israelites to march in the opposite direction. 

- The Red Sea could refer to bodies of water on either side of the Sinai Peninsula (the Gulf of Aqaba or the Gulf of Suez).
Israel’s disobedience brought on the consequences they feared would come from obeying.

The threat of divine punishment for their sins caused the people of Israel to feel grief. Yet, their wills remained rebellious, and they disobeyed the Lord's command again ({{Numbers 14:25|14:25}}). Caleb and Joshua's based their initial confidence on God's promise to be with them ({{Numbers 14:9|14:9}}). Yet, God would not fight with the Israelites until all the rebels had died.
*Because you have turned away from the LORD, He will not be with you:* The prediction of Moses summarizes the entire chapter.
The *ark of the covenant *represented God's presence and blessings (compare {{1 Samuel 4:1-11|1 Samuel 4:1–11}}).
These instructions suggest that the Israelites would eventually live in the promised land ({{Numbers 14:31|14:31}}; {{Numbers 15:18|15:18}}).

Chapters {{Numbers 1:1-14:45|1–14}} cover a short time period, but chapter {{Numbers 15:1-41|15}} marks the start of a long period. This is the main part of the forty years in the wilderness, about which little is known. There are references to events during this time (for example, {{Deuteronomy 8:2-6|Deuteronomy 8:2–6}}; {{Deuteronomy 29:5-6|29:5–6}}; {{Joshua 5:4-8|Joshua 5:4–8}}; {{Ezekiel 20:10-26|Ezekiel 20:10–26}}; {{Amos 5:25-26|Amos 5:25–26}}; {{Acts 7:42-43|Acts 7:42–43}}). 

During this period, Moses continued to give laws to guide Israel’s life as a nation. These laws would be especially important in the future. They were meant for the day when the people who survived the wilderness would enter the promised land. 

This chapter addresses three main types of laws. {{Numbers 15:1-41|Numbers 15}}is in the middle of stories about a stubborn and disobedient Israel. It offers hope that the promised land still waited for the next generation of Israel’s people.

God had made it very clear that the Levites were set apart to serve him. They were to take care of everything that had to do with the holy tent.

He had also made it very clear that males from Aaron’s family line were to be priests. They were responsible for everything that had to do with sacrifices and the altar. This included the special water that made people and things clean.

The Levites and priests wouldn’t receive land or get paid with money. Instead, God provided for them from the offerings given by the other Israelites.

Yet Korah and other Levites who weren’t from Aaron’s family line didn’t like God’s rules. They wanted to be priests. When they spoke against Aaron, they opposed the way that God led his people. God put them to death for this.

Other Israelites blamed Moses and Aaron for the deaths. Yet Moses and Aaron remained faithful to serving the Israelites. Again and again, they prayed for God to have mercy on the Israelites. As a result over and over again God decided not to destroy his people.

God made Aaron’s walking stick produce buds and flowers. This was a sign that the Israelites must respect Aaron and his sons as priests.
*an offering … a pleasing aroma to the LORD:* Honor and thanks through sacrifices and offerings pleases God.
All people in the land, both Israelites and foreigners, were to be equal before the Lord in all matters (see also {{Leviticus 24:22|Leviticus 24:22}}).

These gifts were signs of gratitude to God for the crops he provided. The people were not to give these offerings right away. They were to begin after the Hebrews reached the promised land.

At that time, they would settle there and begin planting crops. Then they would bring these gifts to thank God for the harvest.

Sins done without knowing were treated differently from sins done on purpose ({{Numbers 15:30-31|15:30–31}}). The law also made a difference between the actions of the whole community and the actions of one person (see also {{Leviticus 4:1-5:19|Leviticus 4–5}}).

- Atonement (the way God provides forgiveness and restores a relationship with him) could be made for sins done without knowing or by accident ({{Numbers 15:22-29|15:22–29}}). However, a person who sinned openly and proudly was treated differently (literally *with a high hand;* compare {{Exodus 14:8|Exodus 14:8}}). Such a person showed open disrespect toward God. This was considered blasphemy (speaking against God in a dishonoring way). That person had to face serious consequences (compare {{Leviticus 24:10-16|Leviticus 24:10–16}}; see also {{Deuteronomy 17:2-6|Deuteronomy 17:2–6}}; {{Hebrews 10:26-31|Hebrews 10:26–31}}). 

- *cut off from among his people:* See study notes on Exodus 31:14–15; Leviticus 7:20–21.

This story gives an example of what {{Numbers 15:30-31|Numbers 15:30–31}} teaches. The Sabbath was the Lord’s holy day. The people were not allowed to ignore it or treat it as unimportant ({{Exodus 20:8-11|Exodus 20:8–11}}; {{Exodus 31:14-15|31:14–15}}; {{Exodus 35:1-3|35:1–3}}).

Although it was clear that the man was guilty, the community might have been unsure about his punishment. The death sentence was appropriate because ignoring the Sabbath showed a rejection of God's gracious covenant with Israel ({{Exodus 31:12-17|Exodus 31:12–17}}). It was similar to blasphemy ({{Numbers 15:30|Numbers 15:30}}; {{Leviticus 24:10-16|Leviticus 24:10–16}}; compare {{1 Timothy 1:20|1 Timothy 1:20}}).

- If the Hebrews had remembered their special relationship with the Lord, they might have avoided the problems in Numbers. The *tassels* reminded Israel of their unique bond with a holy God and his expectations. He had freed his people from Egypt. Consistent with his call to a covenant relationship, he expected them to observe the law (see {{Deuteronomy 6:6-9|Deuteronomy 6:6–9}}; {{Matthew 9:20|Matthew 9:20}}; {{Matthew 14:36|14:36}}; {{Matthew 23:5|23:5}}). 

- The color *blue* was a sign of royalty, which means kingship or rule. It also reminded the people of God’s holiness.

Another rebellion demanded a clear separation of duties between priests and Levites. This power struggle was more serious than previous rebellions against God's authority (chapter {{Numbers 11:1-35|11}}; {{Numbers 12:1-15|12:1–15}}; {{Numbers 14:1-45|14:1–45}}). 

In these historical events, the rebels protested minor issues and questioned their leaders' actions. Yet, Moses reminded them that they were actually rebelling against God. As a result, the Israelites suffered deadly consequences for their rebellion.

The rebels "envied Moses, as well as Aaron" ({{Psalm 106:16|Psalm 106:16}}). They claimed Moses and Aaron had overstepped their authority because all Israelites were God's chosen people ({{Exodus 19:6|Exodus 19:6}}). Their protest for equality against Moses and Aaron's authority probably intended to replace it with their own.
*Moses … fell facedown* on the ground to pray (compare {{Numbers 14:5|14:5}}; {{Numbers 16:22|16:22}}). Then he challenged Korah and his followers to a test.

*Take censers: *Korah and his group were to act like priests by burning incense (as in {{Leviticus 16:11-13|Leviticus 16:11–13}}). By doing this, they were claiming the right to serve as priests. God himself would decide who truly had the right to serve in that role.

Chapters {{Numbers 3:1-4:49|3–4}} describe the special ministry duties of the Levites. Aaron's descendants had the priesthood ({{Numbers 3:1-4|3:1–4}}). The rebels complained against the Lord, not Moses or Aaron.

*land flowing with milk and honey:* This phrase repeats the words the spies used earlier to describe Canaan ({{Numbers 13:27|Numbers 13:27}}). In this story, however, the words are used with sarcasm.

The speakers twist the meaning on purpose. They use this phrase to describe Egypt in a positive way. This distorts the truth about life in Egypt, where the Israelites had lived as slaves (see study note on 11:4–15).

- The Israelites were leaving their new homeland because they had rebelled against Moses. He had done everything possible to bring them to that land (chapters {{Numbers 13:1-14:45|13–14}}). 

- *Will you gouge out the eyes of these men?:* They accused Moses and Aaron of trying to mislead the Israelites.
*Do not regard their offering:* Compare {{Psalm 109:7|Psalm 109:7}} and {{Proverbs 28:9|Proverbs 28:9}}.
Moses gave final instructions for a test to see if the Lord would accept the rebels' offering or Aaron's offering.
At the height of the rebellion, the Lord intervened to save Moses and Aaron. Moses and Aaron then prayed for the people.
*had gathered his whole assembly … at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting:* This was either to watch the test or to remove Moses and Aaron from leadership.

The Lord threatened to destroy the entire community because of widespread sin (compare {{Genesis 18:16-33|Genesis 18:16–33}}). Moses and Aaron prayed to limit the Lord's judgment to those guilty of this specific rebellion.

*Do not touch anything that belongs to them: *These men and their belongings were now "set apart for destruction" (see {{Leviticus 27:28-29|Leviticus 27:28–29}}; compare {{Deuteronomy 7:26|Deuteronomy 7:26}}; {{Deuteronomy 13:17|13:17}}; {{Joshua 6:18|Joshua 6:18}}; {{Joshua 7:1-26|7:1–26}}).

- Moses believed that God would deliver justice, and God did so ({{Numbers 16:31-35|16:31–35}}; compare {{1 Kings 18:18-40|1 Kings 18:18–40}}). 

- *into Sheol: *This was the place of the dead in the Old Testament. Sheol describes the realm where people go after death (see {{1 Samuel 2:6|1 Samuel 2:6}}; {{2 Samuel 22:5-6|2 Samuel 22:5–6}}; {{Job 3:20-22|Job 3:20–22}}; {{Psalm 16:10|Psalm 16:10}}; {{Acts 2:27-33|Acts 2:27–33}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:15|1 Corinthians 15:15}}; {{Revelation 20:13-14|Revelation 20:13–14}}).

Korah’s sons did not die at this time ({{Numbers 26:10-11|26:10–11}}). Later, his descendants became gatekeepers and musicians in the temple ({{1 Chronicles 9:19|1 Chronicles 9:19}}, {{1 Chronicles 9:31|31}}; {{1 Chronicles 26:19|26:19}}; {{2 Chronicles 20:19|2 Chronicles 20:19}}; see the titles of {{Psalm 42:1-11|Psalms 42}}; {{Psalm 45:1-49:20|45–49}}; {{Psalm 84:1-85:13|84–85}}; {{Psalm 87:1-88:18|87–88}}).

The 250 Israelite leaders tried to offer incense even though they were not priests. Their fate was like that of Nadab and Abihu, who also offered unauthorized fire before the Lord ({{Leviticus 10:1-2|Leviticus 10:1–2}}). They also shared the same judgment as those who complained about the hardships in the wilderness ({{Numbers 11:1|Numbers 11:1}}; compare {{2 Kings 1:10|2 Kings 1:10}}).

Although the men who used the incense burners were wicked, the vessels themselves were holy and had to be treated with care and respect. The burning coals were also holy and had to be scattered so that they would not be used for any other purpose.

Eleazar made a bronze sheet to cover the altar, replacing or adding to the earlier one ({{Exodus 38:2|Exodus 38:2}}). Like the plain blue tassels in {{Numbers 15:37-41|Numbers 15:37–41}}, it reminded the people of Israel to obey God.
The Israelites continued their self-destructive and defiant behavior, which caused their problems. They then blamed Moses and Aaron for the events.
The *glory of the LORD appeared* again and threatened to destroy the people of Israel (see {{Numbers 16:19-20|16:19–20}}). Moses and Aaron intervened by falling facedown on the ground.
Moses and Aaron quickly acted to save the Israelites from God's anger. Aaron used an incense burner with hot coals among the people to stop the plague.

The shepherd's *staff *was a common item (see {{Psalm 23:4|Psalm 23:4}}). Like the scepter, it symbolized authority (see {{Jeremiah 48:17|Jeremiah 48:17}}). This trial was fitting because the Hebrew words for "staffs" and "tribes" sound the same. The Lord's chosen staff would show his chosen tribe.

The Lord gave another test to make the lesson clear. This test repeated the teaching from the events in chapter {{Numbers 16:1-50|16}}. It also prepared the people for the instructions that follow in chapter {{Numbers 18:1-32|18}}.
The staffs were in the Lord's presence, a safe place where no one could interfere with them ({{Numbers 17:7|17:7}}).

- *Aaron’s staff … produced almonds:* This proved he was God's chosen leader and that the Levites had a special role. The cups on the lampstand of the Tent of the Testimony (the tabernacle) had the shape of almond blossoms ({{Exodus 25:33-36|Exodus 25:33–36}}). Later, the prophet Jeremiah’s vision of an almond branch symbolized the Lord's watchfulness and his plans to act ({{Jeremiah 1:11-12|Jeremiah 1:11–12}}). 

- There is no natural reason for Aaron’s staff to bud. Almond wood is soft when alive and only hardens enough for use as a staff after it has dried.

After each tribal leader claimed his staff, it was clear that Aaron’s deserved special treatment. They placed it permanently in front of the ark of the covenant to warn potential rebels. It would also warn Israelites who complained about the Lord and his appointed leaders. The ark of the covenant eventually contained this staff, a jar of manna, and the stone tablets of the law (compare {{Hebrews 9:4|Hebrews 9:4}}). This was to remind the Israelites of their time wandering in the wilderness.

The Lord and his tabernacle were holy. Because of God's holiness, his holy place could be dangerous for unqualified people. Moses worked hard to help the people understand and respect the God of Israel. His efforts were becoming successful.

The Lord gave special authority to Aaron, his sons (the priests), and his relatives (the Levites). They were responsible to God for offenses against the holy place. Yet, only the priests were responsible to God for their own violations of God's instructions for their service.

The instructions here came from the need shown in chapter {{Numbers 17:1-13|17}} for clear boundaries between the people, priests, and Levites. The Levites had special privileges and important responsibilities. One key part of their job was to protect the Tent of Meeting from unauthorized entry (chapter {{Numbers 16:1-50|16}}).

- *all the duties:* See {{Numbers 1:47-53|1:47–53}}; {{Numbers 3:5-38|3:5–38}}; {{Numbers 4:1-33|4:1–33}}. 

- *they must not come near:* The Levites could approach only after they had covered the holy objects for transport.
Aaron and the priests represented the people in the presence of the Lord. Their actions affected all of Israel (see {{Numbers 16:18-21|16:18–21}}).

Only the priests, who were Aaron and his descendants, could perform holy duties inside the sanctuary or approach the altar. This altar was a holy area that deserved special honor. Only the high priest could serve in the Most Holy Place. The Levites could only serve in the courtyard, away from the altar. The exception was when it was time to assemble or disassemble the Tent of Meeting (chapter {{Numbers 4:1-49|4}}).
*Levites … as a gift to you:* {{Numbers 3:1-4:49|Numbers 3–4}}explains this phrase. See also {{Numbers 3:9|3:9}}; {{Numbers 8:16|8:16}}, {{Numbers 8:19|19}}.

*any outsider … must be put to death: *This verse warned all Israelites to avoid areas where God did not allow them to be. God prohibited access to certain holy places for those not qualified in a religious sense. Only the holiest members of the community could access these holy areas. Ignoring this rule meant risking one's life because it violated God's holiness (see also {{Numbers 1:51|1:51}}, {{Numbers 1:53|53}}; {{Numbers 3:10|3:10}}, {{Numbers 3:29-38|29–38}}; {{Numbers 4:1-20|4:1–20}}).

The priests and Levites received support through the sacrificial system (see, for example, {{Leviticus 7:28-36|Leviticus 7:28–36}}). God's chosen representatives deserve payment for their work (compare {{Matthew 10:9-10|Matthew 10:9–10}}; {{1 Corinthians 9:3-10|1 Corinthians 9:3–10}}).

- Only Aaron and his sons, the priests set apart to serve in God's presence, consumed the most holy offerings ({{Exodus 28:1|Exodus 28:1}}; {{Exodus 29:44-46|29:44–46}}). 

- This portion was a holy offering given to God, and the priests had to treat it with respect ({{Numbers 18:10|Numbers 18:10}}). Other types of offerings provided food for the priests and their families, but only if they were ceremonially clean ({{Numbers 18:11-12|18:11–12}}).

Offerings set apart for the Lord were available to Aaron and his extended family. The Hebrew term here means a thing or person totally set apart to the Lord. This could involve either destroying or giving the person of thing as an offering. This verse speaks of an offering (see {{Leviticus 27:28-29|Leviticus 27:28–29}}).

The Lord supported the Hebrew priests and their families from the offerings set aside for him. The priests received firstborn animal offerings and the redemption fee for Israel’s firstborn sons. People had to redeem both firstborn sons and the offspring of unclean animals with a silver fee, since they could not sacrifice either one (see {{Numbers 3:13|3:13}}, {{Numbers 3:40-51|40–51}}; {{Exodus 13:2|Exodus 13:2}}).

*a covenant of salt: *These arrangements were part of an eternal and unbreakable covenant (see {{2 Chronicles 13:5|2 Chronicles 13:5}}). The agreement was meant to be permanent because salt, a preservative, symbolized permanence ({{Leviticus 2:13|Leviticus 2:13}}).

- The priests and Levites did not have a tribal homeland. They lived scattered among Israel's other tribes (see {{Numbers 35:1-8|35:1–8}}; {{Deuteronomy 12:12|Deuteronomy 12:12}}; {{Joshua 21:1-42|Joshua 21:1–42}}). 

- *I am your portion and your inheritance: *Instead of land, Israel's priests had assurance that God himself would be their homeland. The tribe of Levi received tithes as payment for their holy service.

The Israelites gave a tithe, which was one-tenth of their yearly income (see {{Deuteronomy 14:22-29|Deuteronomy 14:22–29}}; {{Deuteronomy 26:12|26:12}}; {{Nehemiah 10:35-39|Nehemiah 10:35–39}}; {{Malachi 3:8-12|Malachi 3:8–12}}; {{Matthew 23:23|Matthew 23:23}}; compare {{Genesis 14:17-20|Genesis 14:17–20}}; {{Hebrews 7:5-10|Hebrews 7:5–10}}).

The Levites received a tithe (one-tenth) of the goods of the Israelites ({{Numbers 18:24|18:24}}). However, they were not allowed to keep all of it. They also had to give a tithe of that tithe, which means one-tenth of the one-tenth. They gave this portion to the priests as their own harvest offering ({{Numbers 18:27|18:27}}).
Levites and their families could eat any food received as tithes. This food was their payment for working at the Tent of Meeting.
The food tithes were holy gifts from the people of Israel. They could not use these gifts for something common by failing to give a portion to the priests.

They made the water for the purification ceremony with ashes of the red heifer ({{Numbers 19:9|19:9}}). It might be the same as the water of purification in {{Numbers 8:7|8:7}} (see also {{Numbers 31:19-24|31:19–24}}). This ceremony needed the ashes of a red heifer. The color probably represented blood (compare {{Hebrews 9:13-14|Hebrews 9:13–14}}).

This section explains how ordinary Israelites can become ceremonially clean again after touching a corpse and avoid defiling the Tent of Meeting (see {{Numbers 9:4-12|9:4–12}}; {{Leviticus 17:15|Leviticus 17:15}}; {{Leviticus 21:1-4|21:1–4}}, {{Leviticus 21:11-12|11–12}}). God's holiness demands that the place of his presence remains pure and separate from pollution (compare {{1 Corinthians 6:9-11|1 Corinthians 6:9–11}}, {{1 Corinthians 6:18-20|18–20}}).

To protect Aaron’s holy status, Eleazar had to perform the red heifer offering because it caused ceremonial impurity (see {{Leviticus 21:10-12|Leviticus 21:10–12}}). The red heifer ceremony differed from the regular sacrifice (compare {{Leviticus 4:3-12|Leviticus 4:3–12}}).

The only other passage where cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet wool appear together is {{Leviticus 14:1-57|Leviticus 14}}. That chapter describes another ceremony (also "outside the camp") that resulted in ceremonial purification.

Some scholars suggest Eleazar added cedar wood and hyssop for their aroma. Hyssop is associated with purification ({{Exodus 12:22|Exodus 12:22}}; {{Psalm 51:7|Psalm 51:7}}; compare {{Hebrews 9:19|Hebrews 9:19}}). The scarlet yarn, like the red heifer, probably symbolizes blood. Together, the cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet wool symbolize cleansing.

It required three people to produce and collect the heifer’s ashes. These were Eleazar, the person who burned the animal, and the person who gathered its ashes. All three became ceremonially impure for a day because of this process. The same was true for the person who used the finished product. This was a potion made from the ash dust and water (compare {{Numbers 19:21|19:21}}). This potion had the same defiling effect as blood associated with sacrifices ({{Leviticus 6:27-28|Leviticus 6:27–28}}).

The ceremony of burning the red heifer intended to produce ashes. They collected these ashes and stored them in a pure place outside the camp. The Israelites used them in water for purification ceremonies to remove pollution, such as contact with a corpse ({{Numbers 19:11-22|19:11–22}}).

If someone touched a human dead body, that person became ceremonially unclean for seven days (compare {{Leviticus 21:1-3|Leviticus 21:1–3}}). This meant a person was not allowed to take part in worship until they were made clean. 

To become clean again, the person had to use the water of purification. This water was sprinkled on the third day and again on the seventh day.

Becoming unclean by touching a dead body was very serious. A person who was ceremonially defiled (not fit for worship) could also make the Lord’s tabernacle unclean (compare {{Leviticus 15:31|Leviticus 15:31}}). 

Because of this danger, such impurity could lead to being “cut off” from the community of Israel. This meant being removed from the people, and in some cases, it could mean death (see {{Numbers 9:13|Numbers 9:13}}; {{Exodus 12:15|Exodus 12:15}}; {{Leviticus 7:20-21|Leviticus 7:20–21}}; {{Leviticus 17:4-14|Leviticus 17:4–14}}; {{Leviticus 20:17-18|Leviticus 20:17–18}}).

Death made a person ceremonially unclean, and this uncleanness could spread. It could pass to an object or to a place where someone had died (compare {{Leviticus 15:1-12|Leviticus 15:1–12}}). This means that anything connected to the dead body could also become unclean. People had to be careful so that impurity did not spread through the camp.
To cleanse with the heifer's ashes, they made a special purifying mixture. They combined ashes from the burnt purification offering with fresh water (compare {{Numbers 5:17|5:17}}).
Everyone in Miriam's generation also died ({{Numbers 14:26-30|14:26–30}}). This included Moses and Aaron ({{Numbers 20:2-13|20:2–13}}, {{Numbers 20:22-29|22–29}}).

The people of Israel continued to complain and argue as they wandered in the desert. They said it would have been better to remain slaves or to be dead. That is how unhappy they were.
